title: Everyday Illness

learn.summary: Most of what you'll actually handle isn't dramatic — it's fevers, stomach bugs, and the recurring question 'is this ER-worthy?' Getting triage right saves money, time, and occasionally lives in both directions: knowing what can wait, and knowing what absolutely can't. When genuinely unsure, nurse advice lines (many insurers and hospitals run free 24/7 lines) exist precisely for this call.

do: Find and save your insurer's or local hospital's 24/7 nurse advice line number this week.

children.title: Fevers

learn.summary: Fever is a defense, not a disease — treat the person's comfort, not the number. Adult red lines: 103°F (39.4°C) or higher, a fever lasting more than 3 days, or fever with stiff neck, severe headache, rash, confusion, or trouble breathing all warrant medical care. The absolute rule: any fever of 100.4°F (38°C) or more in a baby under 3 months is an immediate call to a doctor or ER — no wait-and-see.

do: Verify you own a working thermometer today — test it, and replace the battery or the device if it fails.

children.title: Dehydration & ORS

learn.summary: For vomiting and diarrhea, oral rehydration solution — a precise balance of glucose and salts that exploits the gut's sodium-glucose co-transport — has saved tens of millions of lives since the 1970s and beats water or sports drinks. Pharmacy ORS packets are cheap; the WHO field recipe is 6 level teaspoons sugar and half a teaspoon salt in 1 liter of clean water. Small frequent sips stay down better than large gulps; escalate if there's no urination for 8+ hours, sunken eyes, or lethargy.

do: Add 2–3 ORS sachets (pharmacy or online) to your medicine cabinet this week — buying them mid-stomach-flu is the wrong time.

children.title: ER vs Urgent Care vs Doctor

learn.summary: ER (or 911): chest pain, stroke signs, severe bleeding, trouble breathing, major trauma, sudden severe headache, suicidal crisis. Urgent care: sprains, minor cuts needing stitches, fevers in otherwise-healthy adults, UTIs, minor burns — typically a fraction of ER cost and wait. Primary care or telehealth: anything that can wait a day or two. The costly mistakes run both ways: ER visits for earaches, and 'sleeping off' chest pain.

do: Look up your nearest urgent care clinic and its hours today, and save it in your phone alongside your nearest ER.
